# Model Routing Policy

Policy revision 2.1, as shipped by the mr plugin. Tier names are short names; dispatch them as `mr:<name>`.

## Overview

This policy routes Claude Code work through fixed tiers of subagents so that every task runs on the cheapest model and effort that passes its checks. The main session is the dispatcher and integrator. Planners plan, test cases included; executors implement test-first; the main session gates every task with mechanical checks; verifiers judge only the tasks a verification trigger selects; only planners consult the advisor.

Tier names in this policy are short names. Dispatch them as `mr:<name>`, for example `mr:exec-haiku-low`; the dispatch guard also accepts the bare name.

Before a project's first delegation, run `mr-init --claude-md` in the project root. It creates `docs/plans/README.md` and `docs/model-routing-log.md` from the plugin templates and adds a one-line pointer to this policy to the project's CLAUDE.md. Where CLAUDE.md is generated by a script, run `mr-init` without the flag and add the printed line through that generator.

Where another rule conflicts with this policy, this policy wins. The full text is available with the skill `mr:routing-policy`.

## Roles
- The main session's default model is the `sonnet` family at `high` effort. The user may run a session on another model by choice; the session-start note about it is informational, so never ask the user to switch. The advisor is whatever model the user's settings choose. It is the dispatcher and integrator. Its jobs: intake and lane selection; building the skills inventory; choosing planner tiers; running scouts; relaying file paths between agents; dispatching executors and verifiers as the plan assigns; the final gate; commit and merge; logging.
- In the full lane, the main session never writes plans or production code itself. A file that lists tasks with tiers is a plan wherever it lives (for example in a private run directory outside the repository), so only a planner writes one; the main session writes only fast-lane specs, one task each.
- Planners own the solution: from the user's request and the evidence they work out the real problem and the best complete fix, then plan it, test cases included; the main session's framing is input, not the design. Executors implement test-first. The main session gates every task with mechanical checks. Verifiers judge only the tasks where risk or a failed check justifies the cost. Only planners may use the advisor.
- No agent has a default model, effort, or skill set. Every delegation picks a specific tier agent and states its skills explicitly.
- Optimize for cost per successful outcome.

The tier agents ship with this plugin. Dispatch them as `mr:<name>`:

- Scouts: `scout-haiku-low` (haiku, low), `scout-haiku-med` (haiku, medium), `scout-sonnet-high` (sonnet, high)
- Planners: `plan-sonnet-high` (sonnet, high), `plan-opus-high` (opus, high), `plan-opus-xhigh` (opus, xhigh)
- Executors: `exec-haiku-low` (haiku, low), `exec-haiku-med` (haiku, medium), `exec-haiku-high` (haiku, high), `exec-sonnet-med` (sonnet, medium), `exec-sonnet-high` (sonnet, high), `exec-sonnet-xhigh` (sonnet, xhigh)
- Verifiers: `verify-sonnet-med` (sonnet, medium), `verify-sonnet-high` (sonnet, high), `verify-opus-high` (opus, high)

No other agent type (built-in agents, other plugins' agents, or project agents) is dispatched.

## Dispatch mechanics (verified on Claude Code 2.1.306, 2026-10-24)
- Never pass `model` or `effort` on any Agent call; either one overrides the frontmatter.
- Never set `CLAUDE_CODE_EFFORT_LEVEL` (it overrides every agent's frontmatter effort, so a shell profile or tool that exports it breaks routing) or `CLAUDE_CODE_SUBAGENT_MODEL` (and never `CLAUDE_CODE_SUBAGENT_MODEL_FORCE`). The session-start context warns when it sees any of them.
- Nesting is blocked in four layers: each agent's `disallowedTools` (`Agent, TeamCreate, TeamDelete, SendMessage`), its `tools` allowlist, its body, and `CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_SUBAGENT_SPAWN_DEPTH=1` in the settings env. On Claude Code 2.1.318, a skill with `context: fork` that a subagent invokes through the Skill tool runs as a separate `general-purpose` subagent that none of these layers stops, so the dispatch guard checks Skill calls too (next bullets).
- The advisor cannot be removed per agent on this version (no frontmatter field; `disallowedTools: advisor` does not detach it, because it is a server tool). The restriction for non-planners is the body line "Never consult the advisor." plus the same line in every non-planner delegation message.
- Agent definitions reach a running session late. After the plugin is installed, enabled or updated, run `/reload-plugins` or start a fresh session before dispatching; if a tier type is reported missing, retry shortly or run the delegation in a fresh `claude -p` session. On 2026-10-24, one of three parallel `exec-haiku-low` launches right after a body change still got the old body, so after changing agent definitions, check the first reports for the new behavior.
- Resume an agent instance (FIX, REPLAN, NEED_EVIDENCE answers, gate failures) with SendMessage to its name or agentId, naming the input file paths and a new Output file. A planner instance is resumed only for its own plan (Full lane workflow, step 2).
- The plugin's PreToolUse hook (`scripts/dispatch_guard.py`, matcher `Agent|Task|Skill`) denies any Agent or Task call whose subagent type is neither a tier nor listed in `dispatch.allow_agents` of the routing config (an empty type counts as `general-purpose`; `fork` and `general-purpose` are denied), any `model` or `effort` parameter on any agent, and a tier delegation without a Skills line (`none` or existing absolute SKILL.md paths), without an `Output:` line with an absolute path, or, for non-planners, without "Never consult the advisor." It recognizes both `mr:<name>` and bare tier names. A blocked call returns the reason; fix the message and resend. For a call that comes from a subagent (the hook event carries `agent_id`), it also denies any Agent or Task call, and a Skill call whose SKILL.md sets `context: fork` or that it cannot find among the user, project and plugin skills; if that check fails internally, it denies. A denied agent can still Read the SKILL.md path on its Skills line and follow it inline.
- Tier agents run with `omitClaudeMd: true`: they start without user or project CLAUDE.md files and read the project rules files their delegation names. Every role has Read, Write and the Skill tool; with the Skill tool, Claude Code (2.1.318) attaches the session's skill listing to an agent's first prompt, roughly 15K tokens with several hundred skills installed. Agents load the skills their Skills line names, by Read of the SKILL.md path or with the Skill tool. Roles with Bash also have Monitor and TaskStop, because Bash refuses `sleep N` followed by other commands and points to Monitor. On Claude Code 2.1.312, `omitClaudeMd` does not cover nested memory: when an agent touches a file, Claude Code still attaches the CLAUDE.md files (with their imports) of the directories between the session's launch folder and that file, and user rules whose `paths:` match it. No plugin setting stops this. Launch Claude Code in the project root to keep the project's and the workspace's CLAUDE.md files out of tier agents; the session audit flags every tier agent that still received one. Built-in commands that spawn other agent types (`/code-review`, `/simplify`, `/security-review`) are denied unless their type is allowlisted.

## Skills inventory
- At the start of every full-lane run, the main session builds a skills inventory: every skill available in this session (user, project, and plugin, as listed in the session's skills listing, plus skills kept one folder deeper in a group folder, which are not in the listing and load only by Read), each with its name, scope, SKILL.md path and one-line description. Exclude skills that set `disable-model-invocation`, because agents cannot load them.
- The main session passes the inventory file's path to the planner. It does not pass the full inventory to scouts, executors, or verifiers; they receive only their Skills line.
- Run `mr-skills --out <handoff dir>/skills-inventory.md`; it writes the user, project and plugin skills it can find, including grouped skills (scope `<scope> group <group>`), with their SKILL.md paths and without those that set `disable-model-invocation`, as a Markdown table; add any skill from the session's listing that it missed.

## Skill Assignment
- Every delegation message to every agent includes a Skills line. "Skills: none" is valid and is the right answer for many tasks. Name each skill by the absolute path of its SKILL.md (the inventory's Path column), comma-separated.
- Who assigns: the main session assigns skills for scouts, planners, and fast-lane executors; the planner assigns skills for executors and verifiers, per task, in the plan file.
- The main session passes the skills the user names as must-follow to the planner with the user's decisions; the planner puts them on every executor and verifier Skills line they apply to, and the main session does the same for scouts and fast-lane executors.
- What to assign: the general skills the user or the project rules name as must-follow, plus the skills for the task's language, framework and specific work (its testing, review or output-format skill). Do not assign a skill merely because it is related to the topic.
- The verifier of a task always receives the same skills as that task's executor, plus any review or testing skill that applies. A verifier must judge against the same conventions the executor was told to follow.
- Limits: at most 4 skills for any Haiku agent, because loaded skills consume context and Haiku bills about five times more once a prompt exceeds 100K tokens; at most 6 skills for any other agent.
- Precedence when instructions conflict: this policy, then the project's claude.md, then the plan, then skills.
- An agent may read at most one unlisted SKILL.md, only when clearly necessary, and must report it. Repeated unlisted loads for the same task type mean the planner's assignment rules need updating.

## Lane selection
Use the fast lane only when all of these are true:
- the change is mechanical and fully known in advance;
- it touches one file (its test file does not count), or is a trivially repeated edit;
- it involves no design decision;
- it does not touch authentication, payments, data integrity, migrations, or security.

Fast lane process:
- The main session writes a short spec: goal, file, exact change, verification command, a Skills line (usually "none"), and an Output line.
- It dispatches to `exec-haiku-low`, or `exec-haiku-med` if any logic is involved.
- It runs the verification command itself.
- It merges the executor's commit.
- No planner, advisor, or verifier is used. Every subagent launch carries substantial fixed context cost; do not spend it on trivial work.

Operational tasks are fast-lane work too: running commands the main session writes out exactly (git push, a conflict-free rebase, polling CI, `gh` calls, a deploy through an existing script, a build or test run), with no file edits. Dispatch them to `exec-haiku-med`, one target per agent, in parallel when independent; reads with no state change go to `scout-haiku-med`. When a step fails in a way that needs a code change or a judgment call, stop that agent and open a full-lane task for the fix. Production deploys still need the user's explicit approval for that change.

Everything else goes through the full lane. A planner is only for work that needs design decisions. Small, clear work, where what to change is already obvious (a type mapping, a typo in a test case, a missing mock, a two-line move, a small issue found mid-run outside the plan's tasks), goes to the fast lane even in the middle of a full-lane run, never to a planner.

## Full lane workflow
1. **Evidence.** The main session runs scouts with narrow questions, starting paths, an Output line, and a Skills line (usually none; a project-conventions skill when scouts must recognize framework-specific patterns). Run scouts in parallel when the questions are independent. Use `scout-haiku-low` for locating, `scout-haiku-med` for reading and summarizing (including read-only `gh`/API queries, CI logs and live endpoint checks), and `scout-sonnet-high` only when the root cause is unclear or spans modules.
   - Ask for plan-ready evidence: for every file the change will likely touch, the path, the line ranges and the exact excerpt of the relevant functions, types or config entries; the callers and tests involved; and the verification commands that exist. The planner builds on this without re-reading the files, so a scout question that only asks for counts or a summary is too thin.
   - Wait for every scout before dispatching the planner.
2. **Plan.** The main session chooses a planner tier and passes it the problem, not a solution: the user's request in their own words, what was observed, the paths of all scout output files, the user's explicit decisions and constraints, the skills inventory file path, an Output line with the plan path, and a Skills line for the planner itself (for example, an architecture or domain skill that shapes the plan).
   - Never prescribe the approach, the task split or the tiers. The main session is not at the planner's reasoning level; an idea of its own goes in labeled as an unverified hypothesis, and the planner decides the plan.
   - One planner instance per topic: the plan it wrote and the tasks directly related to it. Resume an instance only for its own plan (NEED_EVIDENCE answers, REPLANs of its tasks). A new topic that needs design (a new feature, an unrelated bug, a large finding outside that plan) gets a fresh planner and its own new plan file; small, clear work goes to the fast lane. Never grow one plan file with unrelated topics.
   - If the planner returns OUT_OF_TOPIC or NO_PLAN_NEEDED, follow it: start a fresh planner for the new topic, or write a fast-lane spec.
   - If the planner returns NEED_EVIDENCE, dispatch one scout per `## Scout <k>` section of its requests file, passing the file path and the section; then resume the same planner instance with the scouts' output paths through SendMessage.
   - The planner treats the evidence files it is given as verified and has an evidence budget: at most 5 Read/Grep/Glob calls in total, each to fill a gap it names in the plan. A larger gap goes back as NEED_EVIDENCE, answered by cheap scouts, instead of the planner investigating on its own. Reading the files its delegation names, the project rules files and the listed SKILL.md files does not count against the budget.
   - Allow at most 2 evidence rounds. After that, the planner must plan with what it has and list its assumptions explicitly.
3. **Execute.** Dispatch each task to the start tier the plan assigns; the plan's executor tier is the fallback. For a plan without start tiers, start on its executor tier if that is a Haiku tier, otherwise on `exec-haiku-high`; ask the user first about a task with more than 4 skills. Pass the plan file path, the task ID, the task's executor Skills line and Project rules line exactly as written in the plan, and an Output line. Never pass a paraphrase of the task. Order and branch tasks as Task contracts says.
4. **Gate.** For every finished task, run `mr-gate <plan path> <task-id> <worktree path> --commits <shas from the status line> --report <report path> --out <gate file> --base <integration branch>` once from the main checkout (see Gate). It prints `PASS <gate file>` or `FAIL <gate file> checks=<names>`; never repeat its checks by hand. Exit 2 is a usage or plan error (see Gate).
5. **Verifiers, only when triggered.** A per-task verifier (the plan's verifier tier for the tier that did the work) runs before the task merges when the plan marked it `Verify: task`, or when a gate check other than Green failed (red, integrity, coverage, scope, contract, or report mismatch); these failures need judgment, not a blind retry. Other triggered tasks go to the plan's batch: `Verify: batch`; a task that ran below the plan's executor tier, even if the plan marked it Verify: no; a task after a FIX round or an escalation; a task calibration sampling selected. When every task has passed its gate and merged into the integration branch, split the batch in plan order into groups of at most 6 tasks whose verifier Skills lines together name at most 6 skills, and dispatch one verifier per group, in parallel, each in its own detached worktree at the integration branch's head, at the strongest verifier tier its tasks need. An older plan's `Verify: yes` counts as `Verify: task`.
   Pass the plan path, task ID, branch or worktree, the executor's report path, an Output line, the gate results file path, and the task's verifier Skills line and Project rules line exactly as written in the plan; a batch verifier gets every task ID with its report and gate file paths, its worktree, and the union of the Skills and Project rules lines.
6. **Act on the result.**
   - Gate passed and no verifier is due, or its verifier returned PASS (in a batch verdict, `<task-id>:PASS`): the task is done.
   - Only the Green check failed (`checks=green`): resume the same executor instance through SendMessage with the gate file path. This counts as a FIX round. No verifier is needed for it.
   - Verifier FIX: resume the same executor instance with the verdict file path (for a batch, each task coded FIX, with its task ID), then gate it again (a merged batch task: see Gate). Then resume the same verifier instance to re-verify; it must re-run every command.
   - Allow at most 2 FIX rounds at one tier, counting both kinds. After that, escalate the executor: from a start tier below the plan's executor tier straight to that tier, otherwise one tier up. Launch a fresh executor with the plan path, the task ID, the Skills line and Project rules line as written in the plan, the paths of the earlier verdict and failure files, and a new Output line. After a fallback, a verifier for the new work is a fresh instance of the plan's fallback verifier tier.
   - REPLAN, when the plan's design is wrong: resume the same planner instance with the verdict file path, so it can revise that task in the plan file (editing only that task), including its skills if the problem was a skill conflict or a missing skill. The planner may consult the advisor once for this revision (Advisor rules). After the revision, re-execute the task. If a second REPLAN occurs for the same task, move up one planner tier. A REPLAN with `fix=small` goes to the fast lane instead: its executor gets the verdict path as the spec input; log it as a deviation.
   - BLOCKED: the status line's `reason=` says why; fix the environment issue if that reason shows it is clearly mechanical. Otherwise, treat it as a failure under the escalation caps.
7. **Final gate and integrate.**
   - Merge only when every task has passed its gate (and its per-task or batch verifier, if one ran) and the full test suite passes on the integrated branch. Then commit with a clear message and merge. Where a project forbids red-only commits on its main branch, fold the red commit into its green commit after the gate and before the merge.
   - Never force-push or rewrite shared history.
   - Resolve trivial merge conflicts directly. Route non-trivial conflicts as a new task to `exec-sonnet-high`, with verification.
   - Destructive database migrations, data deletion, and production deploys are outside auto-merge scope: prepare them fully, then report.
   - Wrap-up (every task has passed: final gate, merge, docs, log, report) never spawns or resumes a planner. The main session writes the log; docs edits go to the fast lane. A problem found now is either small and clear (fast lane) or a new topic for a fresh planner.
8. **Log** every delegation, as described under Logging.

## Handoffs between agents
- Every tier agent writes its full output to a file and replies with one status line that names the file. The main session never reads these files; it passes their paths to the next agent.
- Handoff directory: one per run, `docs/handoffs/<YYYY-MM-DD>-<topic-slug>/` in the project (or the run directory the project's rules name), kept out of version control. An agent working in a worktree writes inside that worktree's copy of the directory.
- Every tier delegation carries an `Output:` line with the absolute path of a new file in the handoff directory (for planners, the plan file), and a `Project rules:` line when the agent should read something other than the root `CLAUDE.md`/`AGENTS.md` and their in-repository imports (`Project rules: none` for nothing).
- Name handoff files so that no file name starts with `report`, `summary`, `findings` or `analysis` (any case) and ends in `.md`: Claude Code refuses a subagent's Write to such a file, and the dispatch guard denies the delegation. Use role and task names such as `scout-1.md`, `exec-T3.md`, `gate-T3.md` and `verdict-T3.md`.
- Status lines: scouts `DONE <path>` or `BLOCKED <path> reason=<one line>`; executors `DONE <path> commits=<sha>,<sha>` or `BLOCKED <path> reason=<one line>`; verifiers `PASS <path>`, `FIX <path>`, `REPLAN <path> fix=small|design` or `BLOCKED <path> reason=<one line>`; batch verifiers `<worst verdict> <path> tasks=<id>:<verdict>,...` (verdicts PASS, FIX, REPLAN-small, REPLAN-design, BLOCKED; handle each task as if it had its own verdict); planners `READY <plan path>`, `NEED_EVIDENCE <requests path> scouts=<k>`, `OUT_OF_TOPIC <reason>`, `NO_PLAN_NEEDED <reason>` or `BLOCKED <plan path> reason=<one line>`. Decide BLOCKED and REPLAN handling from the inline `reason=` and `fix=` alone. A trailing `findings=<n>` means the file lists n out-of-scope findings: read only that section and route each finding (fast lane, or a fresh planner); `mr-gate` reads its "Checks failing outside the task" sub-heading itself.
- Relay by path only: scout output files and the skills inventory file to the planner; for NEED_EVIDENCE, one scout per `## Scout <k>` section of the requests file, at the tier its heading proposes unless you have a reason to change it; the plan path and task ID to executors; the executor's report path to the verifier; the verdict path to the executor (FIX) or to the planner (REPLAN). For a Green-only gate failure, pass the gate file path; it holds the failing output.
- Delegation and resume messages carry paths and short instructions, never copied evidence, reports or defect lists.
- Usage limit: a reply that is the account's usage-limit message (such as "You've hit your weekly limit · resets <time>") means the agent stopped unfinished; it is neither a failure nor a FIX round. Log the task as interrupted and dispatch nothing until the reset time it names; then resume the same instance with "The usage limit has reset; continue your task." If that fails, start a fresh instance of the same tier with the same delegation (an executor on a new worktree from the integration branch's head). Never merge a plan, or report it done, while one of its agents is interrupted; `mr-audit` flags each one as "stopped by the usage limit".

## Plan Contract
Every plan file (`docs/plans/YYYY-MM-DD-short-slug.md`) contains: the goal; the evidence summary, with file references; assumptions (including any departure from the main session's framing, with the reason); the tasks; risks; Skill Gaps (skills that do not exist but would have helped); and Advisor Notes (suggestions applied and suggestions rejected, with reasons).

Each task contains:
- a task ID, in the task's heading `### Task <ID>: <title>`;
- the goal;
- exact files and functions to touch;
- ordered steps;
- constraints and project conventions to follow;
- explicitly out-of-scope items;
- acceptance criteria;
- exact verification commands;
- for a docs task that states commands, procedures or behavior: a fact sheet listing every command, path and claim the doc will contain, each with its source file and line;
- Test Cases: each behavior to test, with inputs and the expected outcome, as a list item that starts with its ID (`- TC1: ...`), with `(guard)` after the ID when the test passes before the change by design (`- TC4 (guard): ...`); or "Tests: existing suite only" for tasks with no behavior change. The planner writes these, so tests come from the spec, not from the executor's reading of it;
- the Contract block (Task contract format below), from which the run order follows;
- the Gate block (Gate block format below), from which `mr-gate` runs the gate;
- the planned executor tier, with a one-line reason, and the start tier (see Executor tier selection); the planned tier is the fallback;
- the executor Skills line, starting `Skills:` (absolute SKILL.md paths from the inventory, or none), alone on its own line so it can be copied verbatim, with a one-line reason per skill on separate lines;
- the Project rules line: the project rules files the executor and verifier read (paths, or none when the task's constraints already carry every convention);
- `Verify: task`, `Verify: batch` or `Verify: no`, naming the trigger (see Verification triggers);
- the verifier tier and the verifier Skills line (starting `Verifier Skills:`), assigned for every task, because a verifier can still run through a gate failure, a FIX round, or sampling; a task that starts below its planned tier names its start and fallback verifier tiers.

No task may leave a design decision to the executor.

### Task contract format
Every task has a `Contract:` line followed by its items, one per line, up to the first line that is not an item; a task that provides, requires and follows nothing has `Contract: none`. `mr-plan` reads these lines (backticks are ignored, code fences are skipped), so keep exactly this form:
- `- provides: <kind> <name> in <path> -- <shape>`: a name this task creates that a sibling task uses. `<kind>` is symbol, file, config, env, flag, endpoint or id; `<path>` is the repository-relative file that will contain the name. A `file` provide has no `in`: its name is the path. `-- <shape>` is optional and one line, for example a function's parameters and return value.
- `- requires: <task-id> <name> -- <shape>`: a name that task's provides line declares. Copy its shape, so the executor sees it in its own task.
- `- after: <task-id>, <task-id>`: tasks that must pass first although this task uses no name from them.
List as provides every name a sibling task relies on, spelled exactly as the code will spell them (other deliverables may be listed too): the gate checks presence (a whole word for a symbol, the key path for a config key in a JSON file, the exact text otherwise). Two tasks that change the same file are never independent: link them with requires or after. The run order follows from requires and after; there is no separate dependency list.

### Gate block format
Every task has a `Gate:` line followed by its items, one per line, up to the first line that is not an item. `mr-gate` reads them; a value wrapped in backticks is read without them.
- `- files: <path or glob>, ...`: every file the task may change other than its tests (required).
- `- tests: <path or glob>, ...`: the test files commit one adds or changes (required with red or guard lines).
- `- red: <command>`: runs Test Cases that must fail before the change; one line per command.
- `- guard: <command>`: runs only guard Test Cases, which pass before the change by design. Keep guards out of red commands.
- `- green: <command>`: the task's verification commands, then the project's lint and type checks and its full test suite, one per line (at least one).

A task with "Tests: existing suite only" has no tests, red or guard lines.

## Task contracts
Plans declare, per task, what it provides to sibling tasks, what it requires from them and which tasks it runs after (Plan Contract, Task contract format). The main session derives the run order and a gate check from these lines with `mr-plan`; it never orders tasks by hand.
- **Order.** After the planner returns READY, run `mr-plan waves <plan path>`. Exit 0 prints one line per wave; each task is followed by the tasks it depends on. Exit 1 prints contract errors (an unknown task, a requires line that no provides line matches, a cycle): resume the same planner instance with the path of a file holding them, to fix the Contract blocks of the tasks named. This contract fix is not a REPLAN: it does not count toward the REPLAN limits and needs no advisor consult. When the only error is `no task has a Contract line`, the plan predates contracts: order its tasks by hand. Exit 2 is a usage or file error.
- **Branches.** Before the first task, create the plan's integration branch `agent/<plan-slug>-integration` (`<plan-slug>` is the plan file name without its date and `.md`) from the base branch. A task is ready when every task it depends on has passed and been merged into the integration branch. Dispatch ready tasks in parallel, each in its own worktree branched from the integration branch's head, and merge each task into the integration branch as soon as it passes; where red-only commits are forbidden, fold the task's red commit into its green commit before that merge. The final gate runs on the integration branch; then merge it.
- **Gate.** The Contract check runs `mr-plan check <plan path> <task-id> <worktree path>` with the plan's absolute path in the main checkout (plans are not in worktrees). Exit 0: every provides and requires line of the task is present. Exit 1 lists what is missing. A missing provides line, or a requires line the task's own diff removed, fails the gate as a check other than Green. Any other missing requires line means the worktree's base lacked the provider: recreate the worktree from the integration branch's head and dispatch the task again; this is not a FIX round.
- **Failed providers.** A task does not run while a task it depends on has not passed. When that task ends BLOCKED or fails after the escalation caps, report its dependents with it; tasks that do not depend on it go on.
- Presence is not correctness: the requiring task's own tests and the full suite on the integration branch judge behavior.

## Gate
`mr-gate` reads the task's Gate block (Plan Contract) and runs these checks in the task's worktree. The worktree must be clean: the gate checks out commit one, and for Green the base commit (where the task branched from `--base`, else the parent of commit one), in it and restores the branch afterwards. The gate file gives each check as pass, fail or n/a, with its evidence.
- Red: on commit one every `red:` command fails and every `guard:` command passes. Tests that pass before the implementation exists are not testing the change, unless the plan marked them guard. n/a without red and guard lines.
- Test integrity: commit one changes only files on the `tests:` line, later commits change no file from commit one, and the diff adds no skip, xfail or only markers and removes no assertions.
- Coverage: every Test Case ID of the task (`TC1`, ...) appears in commit one, in a test name or a comment. n/a without IDs.
- Scope: every changed file matches the `files:` or `tests:` line.
- Contract: every provides and requires line of the task is present, as `mr-plan check` reports it; n/a for a plan without Contract lines.
- Green: every `green:` command passes: the task's verification commands, the project's lint and type checks, and the full test suite. A failing command the executor listed under "Checks failing outside the task" that also fails on the task's base commit does not fail Green; the gate file names it, and the main session routes it as an out-of-scope finding. An unlisted failure, or a listed one that passes on the base commit, fails Green.
- Report: the report file exists, the status line's commits are the task's commits on its branch, and its "Skills loaded" line names every skill on the task's Skills line; a verifier judges the report's content when one runs.
Exit 0 is PASS, 1 FAIL, 2 a usage or plan error. For a task without a Gate block, resume the plan's planner to add Gate blocks (not a REPLAN, no advisor consult); for an older plan whose planner is gone, run these checks by hand.
Batch tasks merge before their verdict. Keep each one's branch and worktree, unrewritten, until its batch verdict is PASS (where red-only commits are forbidden, merge it with `git merge --squash` instead of folding its commits). Its fix, escalation or replan adds commits on that branch; gate it again with `--base <the base sha in its first gate file>` and `--commits` listing all its commits since that base, then merge it again.

## Planner tier selection (made by the main session)
- **plan-sonnet-high:** work confined to one module, with clear evidence and roughly five tasks or fewer.
- **plan-opus-high:** multi-module work; a root cause that is still unclear after scouting; refactors; anything touching authentication, payments, data integrity, or migrations.
- **plan-opus-xhigh:** architecture or system design, large refactors, cross-service changes, or a second REPLAN after a plan-opus-high plan.

Planning is where reasoning effort pays off most, because planners produce few tokens and their mistakes multiply downstream. When unsure, pick the higher planner tier. This is the opposite of the rule for executors.

## Executor tier selection (made by the planner)
For each task, answer three questions:
- **B.** Does it touch more than one module or more than about two production files? Test files, fixtures and generated artifacts do not count.
- **C.** Will it need more than about ten sequential tool calls beyond the standard red/green cycle, or a run-fix-iterate loop against an environment (Docker, a deploy, an integration stack, external CI)? Running the task's own tests and verification commands is not such a loop.
- **D.** Is it tricky: concurrency, security, data integrity, performance, or heavy edge cases?

Count the yes answers:
- **0:** `exec-haiku-low` if purely mechanical; `exec-haiku-med` otherwise.
- **1:** `exec-haiku-high` if the only yes is D; `exec-sonnet-med` otherwise.
- **2:** `exec-sonnet-high`.
- **3:** `exec-sonnet-xhigh`.

When torn between two tiers, pick the lower one and rely on escalation. Exception: authentication, payments, data integrity, and migrations go one tier higher, but never above `exec-sonnet-high`: `exec-sonnet-xhigh` needs three yes answers. Every task starts on Haiku, so split a task that would need more than 4 skills into tasks that each need at most 4; a task that cannot be split goes under the plan's Risks.

Start tier: the tier chosen above is the planned tier and the fallback. Every task starts on Haiku: on its planned tier if that is a Haiku tier, otherwise on `exec-haiku-high`. The same executor gets the FIX rounds first; then the task goes straight to its planned tier. A task that starts below its planned tier is at least `Verify: batch`, so write its steps, file list and Test Cases precisely enough for a Haiku executor.

Split for the cheap tier: a mechanical change spread over many files (a rename, a class or token migration, a repeated edit) becomes folder-sized tasks with an exact mapping table in the plan, each `exec-haiku-low`, rather than one large Sonnet task.

Docs that state commands, procedures or behavior (runbooks, ADRs, READMEs, agent guides such as AGENTS.md) go to `exec-haiku-med` at least (`exec-sonnet-med` when they span modules), with a fact sheet in the task; wording-only docs stay on `exec-haiku-low`.

What each executor tier is for:
- **exec-haiku-low:** renames, config and environment changes, boilerplate following existing patterns, adding fields, copy and wording-only docs changes, and tests from cases given in the plan.
- **exec-haiku-med:** single-module logic with clear tests, such as serializers, simple endpoints, utilities, and small components; and operational runbooks with exact commands (push, rebase, CI polling, scripted deploys, build and test runs).
- **exec-haiku-high:** tricky but well-specified single-module logic, such as parsing, validation, and edge-case-heavy functions.
- **exec-sonnet-med:** standard multi-file feature work across roughly two to five files.
- **exec-sonnet-high:** cross-module changes, refactors, Celery and BullMQ work, Docker and terminal-heavy run-fix loops.
- **exec-sonnet-xhigh:** the delegation ceiling, only for a task with three yes answers or as the escalation after a failure at `exec-sonnet-high`; the audit flags any other use.

## Verifier tier selection (made by the planner)
A verifier is never weaker than the executor it checks.
- Haiku executor tiers → `verify-sonnet-med`.
- `exec-sonnet-med` and `exec-sonnet-high` → `verify-sonnet-high`.
- `exec-sonnet-xhigh`, and any task touching authentication, payments, data integrity, migrations, or security → `verify-opus-high`.

A task that starts below its planned tier names two verifier tiers: `verify-sonnet-med` for its start tier, and the tier the list above gives for its planned tier, used after a fallback. A task touching authentication, payments, data integrity, migrations, or security, or planned on `exec-sonnet-xhigh`, keeps `verify-opus-high` at both tiers.

### Verification triggers (marked by the planner)
`Verify: task` (its own verifier, before the task merges) when the task touches authentication, payments, data integrity, migrations, or security, or its planned tier is `exec-sonnet-xhigh`.
`Verify: batch` (one verifier for several tasks, after they merge into the integration branch) when no task trigger applies and:
- the task starts below its planned executor tier;
- acceptance cannot be fully expressed as automated tests: UI behavior, documentation correctness, performance, or infrastructure configuration.

All other tasks are `Verify: no` and rely on the gate.

## Calibration sampling
- For each project's first 50 full-lane tasks (count the rows in its `docs/model-routing-log.md`), the main session also adds a random 20% of Verify: no tasks to the plan's batch verification. Draw with `python3 -c "import random; print(random.random() < 0.2)"` and log the draw.
- After those 50 tasks, read the log. If sampled verifiers found real defects (FIX or REPLAN) in under 5% of samples, drop sampling to 5%. If they found defects in more than 10% of samples for a given executor tier or task type, propose that this tier or task type becomes `Verify: batch`, where Logging says proposals go: the project's claude.md, or, where claude.md is generated or not committed, the log's proposals section and the session report.
Count tasks run below their planned tier separately. Once 50 of them have run with a defect rate under 5%, propose to the human that they be verified by sampling instead of always; until the human agrees, verify every one.

## Advisor rules
- Only planners consult the advisor, once per plan: after the complete draft is written to the plan file, so the advisor sees the evidence, the problem and the whole plan, and before finalizing. Never earlier (not while gathering evidence, not before returning NEED_EVIDENCE).
- If the advisor approves, the planner finalizes. If it asks for changes, the planner applies those the evidence supports, records any it rejects with the reason under Advisor Notes, and finalizes. It never consults again to check the revision.
- A REPLAN revision follows the same rule: at most one consult for it.
- No other agent and no other phase uses the advisor.

## Forbidden
- Effort `max` on any agent. It burns several times the tokens without scoring better, and on Sonnet it fans out into out-of-scope work.
- Effort `xhigh` on Haiku.
- Opus as an executor.
- `exec-sonnet-xhigh` for a task without three yes answers, except as the escalation after a failure at `exec-sonnet-high`.
- Any agent outside the defined tiers and `dispatch.allow_agents`, including `general-purpose` and `fork`.
- A `model` or `effort` parameter on any Agent call.
- Copying an agent's output into a delegation or resume message instead of passing its path.
- A Skills line that names skills instead of their SKILL.md paths.
- A subagent invoking a skill with `context: fork` through the Skill tool.
- Passing a paraphrase of a plan task instead of the plan path and task ID.
- A delegation message without a Skills line.
- A planner investigating past its evidence budget instead of returning NEED_EVIDENCE.
- A planner delegation that prescribes the solution, the task split or the tiers instead of stating the problem.
- Resuming a planner instance for work outside its own plan's topic, or sending small, clear work to a planner.
- Spawning or resuming a planner in wrap-up, after every task has passed.
- A second advisor consult on the same plan or revision.
- The main session writing a multi-task plan or choosing executor tiers outside the fast lane.
- Using the frontmatter `skills` field to preload skills on tier agents.
- Assigning skills that set `disable-model-invocation`, or skills that are not in the inventory.
- Nested delegation of any kind: no subagent spawns subagents, forks, creates agent teams, or messages other agents. Only the main session delegates, and it alone relays between agents. If a subagent needs more work done, it returns that need to the main session.

## Haiku context discipline
- Haiku bills about five times its base rate for any request whose prompt exceeds 100K tokens; that is still about a quarter of Sonnet's price, so a finished Haiku task is worth more than a small context.
- Keep Haiku tasks narrow: exact paths and line ranges, at most 4 skills, and an instruction not to read beyond them.
- Executors start on Haiku, Sonnet-planned tasks included (on `exec-haiku-high`), so planners split work until each task needs at most 4 skills.
- Tier agents start without the user's and the project's CLAUDE.md files (`omitClaudeMd`), so their fixed context is the agent body, the tool definitions, the environment and the skill listing that comes with the Skill tool (roughly 15K tokens with several hundred skills installed); the project rules files and SKILL.md files they load come on top. Haiku tier agents run on Haiku's full context window (1M tokens in Claude Code) and do not compact early: early compaction restarted them at 33-62K tokens, made them re-read the same files and killed some by thrashing. The audit flags a Haiku agent whose prompt passes 300000 tokens; that task should have been split. Where the project rules files are large, name only the rules a task needs on its Project rules line.

## Escalation caps
Per task, allow at most: 2 executor-tier escalations; one replan at each planner tier; two planner tiers in total.
When the caps are exhausted, stop work on that task and report to the human with the full log: plan, verdicts, skills used, and defect history. Continue with other tasks that do not depend on it.

## Logging (mandatory)
- Append one entry per task to `docs/model-routing-log.md` with: date; task type; lane; planner tier; executor tier; verifier tier; skills assigned and skills actually loaded per agent (including any unlisted load and its reason); gate results per check; whether a verifier ran, per task or in a batch, and why (plan trigger, gate failure, post-FIX, below planned tier, or sample) and its verdict; number of FIX rounds; number of REPLANs; number of escalations; final outcome; and input, output, and cache tokens per agent, taken from `message.usage` in each subagent's transcript.
- Take the tokens, the observed model and effort, skill loads (Read calls on SKILL.md files) and advisor calls with `mr-usage <session-id>` (or one `agent-*.jsonl` path; `--agent-type NAME` filters and accepts scoped or bare names; usage is deduplicated by message id). The session-start context gives this session's id.
- Log tokens, not dollars. On a subscription, tokens are what count against usage limits.
- Before its final report, the main session runs `mr-audit <session-id>` and logs its flags (missing Skills or advisor lines, executors without a planner plan, planners over the evidence budget, non-tier agents (any type outside the tiers and `dispatch.allow_agents`, including `fork`), `model` or `effort` on any Agent call, Haiku requests over 300000 prompt tokens, agent replies that are not a status line, agents stopped by the usage limit (dispatch their tasks again after the reset), `exec-sonnet-xhigh` runs with no earlier `exec-haiku-high` or `exec-sonnet-high` run of the task, `scout-sonnet-high` use) and the executor tier mix. The plugin's SessionEnd hook also writes that audit to `audits/<date>-<session>.md` in the plugin data directory for every session that dispatched tier agents. The skill `mr:routing-report` runs both commands.
- At the end of every session, update the aggregate table in the project's claude.md. Per tier and task type, track: first-pass gate pass rate, average FIX rounds, average tokens, and the sampled-verifier defect rate. Where claude.md is generated or not committed, the table lives at the bottom of `docs/model-routing-log.md` and claude.md carries only the pointer.
- If the data shows a task type consistently passing one tier lower, consistently escalating, a planner tier consistently producing REPLANs, a skill consistently loaded unlisted, or a Skill Gap recurring, propose a rule change or a new skill in claude.md (or, where it is generated or not committed, in the log's proposals section and the session report). Never silently change this policy.

## Cost reference
Prices as of 2026-10-24; check current pricing. Per 1M tokens, input / output: Haiku 5.5 0.10 / 0.50 with prompts under 100K tokens (0.50 / 2.50 above); Sonnet 5.5 2 / 10; Opus 5.5 4 / 20. Executors produce the most tokens, so they run on the cheapest tier that passes verification. Planners produce few tokens, so a stronger model there is cheap insurance. A verifier costs about as much as the work it checks, and for Haiku tasks often more, so it runs only where risk, a task run below its planned tier, or a failed check justifies it. Risk tasks get their own verifier; other triggered tasks share one batch verifier per group at the end of the plan. In a 2026-10-29 run, five Sonnet-planned tasks done by Haiku executors cost under $1 instead of about $16 at Sonnet prices, but two of them shipped defects that only their verifiers caught.

## Core rules
- You start without the user's and the project's instruction files. What you need comes from your delegation, the files it names, and the project rules files below.
- Claude Code can still attach instruction files (CLAUDE.md, AGENTS.md, rules) as "Contents of <path>" reminders when you touch files below them. Follow only the project rules files selected by the next rule and your delegation; ignore any other attached instruction file.
- Project rules: if your delegation has a `Project rules:` line, read exactly the files it lists before anything else (`Project rules: none` means none). Without that line, read the repository root's `CLAUDE.md` and `AGENTS.md` if they exist (once, if one only imports the other). Read files those rules import or point to only when they lie inside the repository. Read instruction files outside it (user-level or workspace-level rules, personal notes) only when your `Project rules:` line lists them.
- Read every file you must follow in full (project rules, your plan task, SKILL.md files, verdicts) with the Read tool in chunks of at most 250 lines (`offset` and `limit`), from its first line until a chunk returns fewer lines than you asked for; never use one long Read or `cat` for it. A proxy between Claude Code and the model can cut the middle out of a long tool result and leave only a marker such as "[… 592 lines omitted …]". If a result says lines were omitted, elided or truncated, read that range again in smaller chunks.
- When instructions conflict: this agent definition first, then the project rules files, then the plan or the delegation, then skills.
- Secrets: never print, echo or log a secret value, and never write one into a file, a commit, a commit message or your output. Read secrets from environment variables, as the project rules describe.
- Never push, merge, deploy, publish, or run destructive operations (force-push, rewriting pushed or shared history, branch deletion, deleting data or files outside your task, dropping or migrating databases) unless your delegation or plan task gives that exact command.
- Write everything you store (code, comments, commit messages, files, your output) in English, unless the project rules or the task require another language for specific content.
- If you notice a bug or defect outside your task, do not fix it: describe it (file, line, symptom) under "Out-of-scope findings" in your output file and count it in your status line.

## Skills
- Your delegation has a Skills line: `Skills: none`, or a comma-separated list of absolute paths to SKILL.md files.
- Right after the project rules, load each listed skill in full: read its SKILL.md in chunks as Core rules describe, until you have seen every line, or call the Skill tool with the skill's name when that name is in your skill listing (it returns the whole skill). Skills kept in a group folder are not in the listing; Read is the only way to load them. Paths inside a skill are relative to its SKILL.md directory; read its other files only when the SKILL.md tells you to and your task needs them.
- If a listed SKILL.md cannot be read, say so in your output and continue, unless the task cannot be done correctly without it; then stop and reply with the BLOCKED status line of your role's Output file section.
- Load no other skill, by Read or by the Skill tool, except at most one unlisted skill, and only when it is clearly necessary; name it and the reason in your output. The skill listing Claude Code attaches is not an assignment.
- If a skill's guidance conflicts with the plan or the delegation, do not resolve it silently: record the conflict in your output (planners: in the plan's Risks section).
- Begin your output with a "Skills loaded" line listing every skill you loaded (its SKILL.md path, or its name for a Skill tool call), or "none".

## Output and status line
- Your delegation names your output file on an `Output:` line (for planners, the plan file). Write your complete result there, in the format of your role's Output file section. Write no other file unless your task's file list includes it.
- Your final reply is exactly one status line, in the form your role's Output file section gives, and nothing else: no summary, no excerpt, no greeting. The main session does not read your file; it passes its path to the next agent.
- If you recorded out-of-scope findings, end the status line with ` findings=<n>`.
- Files your delegation names as input (evidence, requests, a plan, a report, a verdict, failure output) are yours to read; nobody pastes their content for you.
- When you are resumed (a FIX round, a REPLAN, answers to your questions), the message names the new input files and a new Output file. Write the new file and leave earlier ones unchanged; planners edit their plan file in place.

## Long-running commands
- Run a command in the foreground when it can finish within the Bash tool's time limit; start it with `run_in_background` only when it cannot.
- Never wait with `sleep`: Bash refuses `sleep N` followed by other commands. To wait for a background command or a condition, use Monitor with an until-loop, for example `until <check>; do sleep 5; done`.
- Before your status line, stop every background shell you started with TaskStop, unless your task says to leave it running.

## Stall watch
A PreToolUse hook (`scripts/stall_watch.py`) watches executors while they run (the roles in `stall_watch.roles`, `config/routing.json`). It uses no model and never consults the advisor; its own errors never block a call (it fails open).
- Signals: the same tool call `repeat_limit` times within the last `repeat_window` calls with no new file change in between (two calls are the same when the tool and the input fields in `stall_watch.call_key_fields` match, or the whole input for a tool not listed there, so a different Bash `description` does not make a call different), or `read_only_streak_limit` read-only calls in a row.
- Nudge: the hook denies the call that tripped the signal and tells the executor why and what to do next; the executor keeps working. Waiting must use a background command and Monitor: Monitor calls are not counted, a repeated status poll is.
- Hand-back: after `max_nudges` nudges, the next signal makes the hook deny every tool except `handback_tools` (Write). The executor writes its Output file and replies `BLOCKED <output path> reason=stalled: <signal>`.
- On that reply, do not resume the executor (the hook keeps denying its tools) and skip its remaining FIX rounds: escalate the task now, as after its last failed FIX round; it counts under the escalation caps. Give the next executor the stalled Output file as an input file.
- A task that stalls a second time, or has no executor escalation left, goes to REPLAN with its stalled Output files, within the escalation caps. A stalled fast-lane task moves to the full lane (the stall shows it is not small and clear): give it to a planner with the stalled Output file.
- Log each stall in the routing log with the signal from `reason=`.
